title: How Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs) Work and How to Prepare
content:
For decades, the government lets you delay taxes in your 401(k) and Traditional IRA. But eventually, the IRS wants its money. Starting at age 73, you are forced to withdraw a specific percentage of your tax-deferred accounts every year, whether you need the money or not. These are **Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs)**. If you have saved a large nest egg, RMDs can push you into a higher tax bracket, trigger surcharges on Medicare premiums (IRMAA), and create a massive tax bill. This guide explains how to forecast and minimize the damage.

Key Takeaways

  • The Age Rule: RMDs currently start at age 73 (rising to 75 in 2033). You must take the first withdrawal by April 1 of the year after you turn 73.
  • The Penalty: If you miss an RMD, the penalty is up to 25% of the amount not withdrawn. It is one of the harshest penalties in the tax code.
  • The Tax Impact: RMDs count as ordinary income. A $50,000 RMD on top of Social Security could push you from the 12% to the 22% tax bracket.
  • Roth Exemption: Roth IRAs have NO RMDs during your lifetime. Moving money from Traditional to Roth before age 73 is the primary defense strategy.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The RMD divisor is based on life expectancy. At 73, you withdraw ~3.65%. At 80, it's ~5.3%. At 90, it's ~8.8%. The percentage rises every year, forcing larger taxable events as you age.

The RMD Formula

How to calculate what you owe.

The Calculation

Balance of all Traditional IRAs on Dec 31 of prior year divided by Life Expectancy Factor (IRS Pub 590-B).

Example:
Account Balance: $1,000,000.
Age: 73 (Factor 26.5).
RMD: $1,000,000 / 26.5 = $37,735.

The Problem: You must take this $37,735 and pay income tax on it. If you don't need it for living expenses, you just have to reinvest it in a taxable account (less efficient).

The 'Tax Torpedo'

This extra $37k income might cause 85% of your Social Security benefits to become taxable, effectively doubling your marginal tax rate. This is the 'Social Security Tax Torpedo'.

Strategies to Lower RMDs

  1. Roth Conversions (Age 60-72): The 'Golden Window'. After you retire but before RMDs start, your income is low. Convert Traditional IRA chunks to Roth IRA to fill up the 12% or 22% bracket. You pay tax now to avoid RMDs forever.
  2. QCDs (Qualified Charitable Distributions): If you are 70.5+, you can send up to $105,000/year directly from your IRA to a charity. This counts as your RMD but is not taxable income. It is the best way to give.
  3. QLAC (Qualified Longevity Annuity Contract): You can use up to $200k of IRA money to buy a longevity annuity. This removes that money from the RMD calculation until age 85.
  4. Work Longer: If you are still working at 73 and don't own >5% of the company, you can delay RMDs from your current 401(k) until you retire.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do Roth 401(k)s have RMDs?

No longer. Secure Act 2.0 eliminated RMDs for Roth 401(k)s starting in 2024. Roth accounts are now safe zones.

Can I aggregate RMDs?

For IRAs, yes. You can calculate the total across 5 IRAs and take it all from one. For 401(k)s, no. You must take an RMD from each specific 401(k) plan.

What if I don't need the money?

You still have to take it. Reinvest it in a taxable brokerage account. Or give it away via QCD to avoid the tax hit.
